summary: In Greek mythology, Actaeon was the son of the herdsman Aristaeus in Boeotia and, through his mother Autonoë, a member of the ruling House of Cadmus, making him a famous Theban hero. Like Achilles in a later generation, he was trained as a hunter by the centaur Chiron. He fell victim to the wrath of Artemis: the hunter became the hunted, transformed into a stag and torn apart by his own raging hounds.

sections.heading: Story
paragraphs: Several versions of Actaeon's transgression survive. In the account adopted by Callimachus, Artemis was bathing in the woods when Actaeon stumbled upon her and stared, amazed at her beauty. The goddess forbade him speech, for if he tried to speak he would be changed into a stag. Hearing the cries of his hunting party, he called out, was instantly transformed, and fled into the woods. Catching sight of his reflection in a pool, he groaned; his own hounds, failing to recognize their master, pursued him, and he was torn to pieces while the gods ignored his plight.

Other sources give different offenses. The Hesiodic Catalogue of Women and Apollodorus's Bibliotheca say his crime was rivaling Zeus for Semele; Euripides's Bacchae has him boast that he was a better hunter than Artemis; Diodorus Siculus reports that he wished to marry the goddess. Some accounts make the hounds Artemis's own dogs.

Ovid's Latin version sets the death on Mount Cithaeron and names fifty hounds. The scholar Lamar Ronald Lacy reconstructed the myth's development across periods: archaic versions involved the rivalry over Semele, classical versions stressed the hunting boast, and Hellenistic versions featured the bathing scene.

sections.heading: The "bed of Actaeon"
paragraphs: The second-century traveler Pausanias reported a spring in Attica near Plataea called the "bed of Actaeon," where it was said he slept when weary from hunting and into which he looked while Artemis bathed.

At Orchomenus a tradition told of a harmful specter haunting a stone. When consulted, the Delphic oracle instructed the people to bury Actaeon's remains and fasten a bronze copy of the specter to the stone with iron, after which annual funeral rites were performed for him as a hero.

sections.heading: Parallels in Akkadian and Ugaritic poems
paragraphs: The Epic of Gilgamesh (tablet vi) offers a parallel: Gilgamesh describes how Ishtar mistreated her lovers, including a herdsman she turned into a wolf, whose own herd-boys hunt him down and whose dogs tear at his haunches.

The Ugaritic hero Aqht, torn apart by eagles incited by Anath because of his hunting bow, likewise parallels Actaeon's fate. Although the virgin Artemis differs from the promiscuous Ishtar, the mythologist T. C. W. Stinton connected Artemis's shooting of Orion with her punishment of Actaeon.

sections.heading: Symbolism regarding Actaeon
paragraphs: Actaeon has been read as a symbol of ritual human sacrifice, in which the dogs represent the sacrificers and Actaeon the victim. He may also stand for human curiosity or irreverence.

Some interpreters have seen in him spiritual transformation or enlightenment. Because his transformation gives him antlers, Actaeon also became a common emblem of the cuckold, an allusion found in Shakespeare's The Merry Wives of Windsor, Robert Burton's Anatomy of Melancholy, and other works.

sections.heading: Cultural depictions
paragraphs: Actaeon appears frequently in classical and Renaissance art, which usually shows either the moment of transgression and transformation or his death by his own dogs. The story was a favorite subject of ancient tragic poets, including Aeschylus, and a notable marble group survives in the British Museum.

In later art and music the myth was treated by Titian (Death of Actaeon and Diana and Actaeon), Marc-Antoine Charpentier (the pastorale Actéon), Henry Purcell, Giordano Bruno, Giambattista Marino, and Jacques Offenbach, whose Orpheus in the Underworld casts Actaeon as Diana's lover. The Diane and Actéon Pas de Deux from Petipa's ballet, with music by Drigo and Pugni, entered the repertoire of La Esmeralda.

Modern writers and artists who reworked the myth include Percy Bysshe Shelley, Ted Hughes (Tales from Ovid), Seamus Heaney, Christopher Marlowe (Edward II), Paul Manship, the French collective LFKs, Matthew Barney (the 2019 film Redoubt), and the songwriter Dar Williams.
